## The problem

- Digital soil mapping now has many "frontier" methods: causal inference,
  deep learning, graph networks, quantum kernels.

- They are rarely compared under one protocol, and their predictions are
  rarely reported with calibrated uncertainty.

- So a simple question usually goes unanswered: is any of them actually better
  than a random forest?

## A conceptual worry: causality

- Variable importance in a predictive model is routinely read as evidence that
  a covariate *causes* the soil property.

- Zhang and Wadoux (2026) argue causal inference in DSM needs conditions that
  observational soil data rarely meet.

- Tempting shortcut: can a learned representation act as an instrument and
  rescue causal identification? We test it directly.

## edaphos

- One R framework, ten method families.

- Every method returns the same object -- a posterior.

- One calibration scorer for all of them: CRPS, interval coverage, width.

- That common currency is what makes a like-for-like comparison possible.

## The test

- 1095 real WoSIS topsoil organic-carbon profiles, Brazilian Cerrado.

- Covariates from WorldClim, SoilGrids, Copernicus tree cover.

- Spatially blocked cross-validation, matched ensemble budgets.

- Scored against the achievable null: each fold's training-fold mean.

## Result 1 -- the benchmark

\centering

| Method                    | RMSE  | R^2    |
|:--------------------------|:-----:|:------:|
| OLS (DAG covariates)      | 0.583 | 0.069  |
| Random forest             | 0.592 | 0.044  |
| Bayesian spatial          | 0.603 | 0.020  |
| Foundation + forest       | 0.616 | -0.013 |
| Quantum kernel            | 0.663 | -0.185 |
| Graph attention           | 0.680 | -0.346 |

\raggedright
\vspace{1em}

Lower RMSE better; R^2 above 0 beats the null.

## Result 1 -- what it says

- A plain OLS on DAG-selected covariates is the most accurate and
  best-calibrated method.

- The three deep or exotic methods fall *below* the achievable null.

- The quantum kernel is the least accurate, and about 300 times slower.

- Elaboration did not pay, here.

## Result 2 -- causal associations

- Backdoor adjustment returns *associations with sensitivity bounds*, not
  identified causal effects.

- Precipitation and clay: robust and significant (robustness value 0.16-0.18).

- Tree cover: naive 2.86, adjusted 0.35 once climate is controlled for.

- The raw tree-cover "effect" was mostly shared climatic confounding.

## Result 3 -- a negative IV result

- We trained a real foundation-model encoder and used its embedding as an
  instrument for precipitation.

- The instruments are very strong: first-stage F about 4630.

- But they fail the validity test: Sargan p about 3e-13.

- A representation that captures everything cannot satisfy the exclusion
  restriction. It is the wrong tool.

## What it means

- Not "deep learning cannot work" -- the sample and signal are small, and a
  linear model on good covariates is hard to beat at this scale.

- A matched, calibration-aware protocol *shows* this; an accuracy-only,
  single-method report hides it.

- Backdoor adjustment is useful, but honest about what it returns.

- The learned-representation shortcut to identification is exactly wrong.

## Conclusion

- The contribution is not a new best predictor.

- It is a reproducible apparatus for asking *which* method helps -- and the
  discipline to say plainly when none does.

- Every number in this talk is regenerated from the bundled data.
